article.title: Is It Social Anxiety, or Is It What Already Happened to You?
article.body:
The avoidance looks the same from the outside. The source is different.

If your attention is already drifting, or you just want the short version: it is at the bottom under The Cliff Notes. Skip ahead. That is what it is there for.

She has been told she has social anxiety since she was nineteen. A counselor at the college health center said it, kindly and in about twenty minutes, and it stuck. She is thirty-four now. She has done cognitive behavioral therapy twice. She has been on two different medications. Both helped some.

She still leaves parties after forty minutes. She still rehearses phone calls. She still cannot eat in front of people she does not know well, and she has built a whole professional life that requires very little of her in a room.

The treatment was aimed at the wrong thing, and nobody ever asked the question that would have caught it.

Why these two get confused

From the outside, social anxiety and post-traumatic stress can produce nearly identical behavior. Both avoid. Both scan. Both light up the body in a room full of people. Both improve when the person leaves, which is exactly the pattern that keeps the avoidance in place.

If you are assessing from behavior alone, you will get this wrong a reasonable percentage of the time, and behavior alone is what a short appointment gives you.

The difference is in what the body is responding to.

Social anxiety is anticipatory. The feared event has not happened. It is a prediction, and the content of the prediction is specific: I will be judged, I will be found lacking, they will see something is wrong with me. The fear is about evaluation, and it is oriented forward.

Post-traumatic stress is a recording. The body already has the data, it filed the data as still-happening, and the response is a re-experiencing. The cue in the room is a smell, a tone of voice, a man standing between her and the door, the particular volume of a crowd.

One is fear of something that has not occurred. The other is a nervous system that has already been through it and did not get the memo that it ended.

The questions that actually separate them

These are the ones I ask, and you can ask them of yourself.

What exactly are you afraid will happen? In social anxiety the answer is coherent and about judgment: I will say something stupid, my hands will shake and they will notice, they will think I am boring. In trauma the answer is frequently vague, or absent, or the person says something like "I do not know, I just cannot" and looks puzzled. Absence of a specific feared outcome is meaningful data.

When does the body react? Social anxiety front-loads. The worst part is often the two days before and the drive there. Once the person is in it and nothing catastrophic has happened, it frequently eases. Trauma responses are more likely to be triggered inside the situation, by a specific cue, and to arrive without warning. Someone who is fine at the party until a particular thing happens is telling you something different from someone who vomited beforehand.

Does it generalize the way it should? Social anxiety is reasonably consistent across similar situations. Trauma responses can be wildly situation-specific in a way that looks illogical: fine at large loud parties, unable to be in a small quiet room with one man.

Is there an index event, and did the avoidance start after it? This sounds obvious. It is skipped constantly, because clinicians ask "any history of trauma" and the person says no, because they are thinking of combat or assault and not of the four years their father was unpredictable in the kitchen.

What is the sleep doing? Nightmares, waking at the same hour, hypervigilance in the house at night. Social anxiety produces the sleeplessness of rehearsal. Trauma produces the sleeplessness of guarding.

The version that is actually hard

Everything above assumes it is one or the other. In practice, in my office, it is usually neither cleanly, and the woman I described at the top is the standard case.

Three things are frequently tangled together, and any of them alone gets read as social anxiety.

The first is developmental trauma: a childhood in which reading other people accurately was a functional requirement, where a shift in a parent's tone predicted something. That produces an adult who monitors faces continuously and gets tired in ways that make no sense to her, and who has no index event to report because it was the weather.

The second is autism, and this is the one most often missed in women. Social exhaustion that comes from processing load and masking is depletion. The party drains her, because she is running conscious calculation on things other people do automatically, and she has been doing it since kindergarten. The behavior looks like avoidance. The mechanism is a battery. Ask what the leaving feels like: the socially anxious person usually feels relief, and the autistic person often feels the way you feel after moving furniture.

The third is accurate learning. If social situations have genuinely gone badly for years, because she was missing cues, or because people did respond poorly, then the expectation of a bad outcome is a well-calibrated prediction. Cognitive therapy aimed at challenging the distortion will fail, and it should, because there is no distortion to challenge. This is where a lot of treatment quietly stalls and the person concludes she is treatment-resistant.

Any two of these can occur together. All three commonly do.

Why getting it right changes the treatment

The three pictures need different first moves, and the wrong first move can make things worse.

Social anxiety responds well to graded exposure with the cognitive work attached. You go into the feared situation, you stay long enough for the prediction to be disconfirmed, and the learning happens because the predicted disaster fails to occur.

Run that same protocol on someone with untreated post-traumatic stress and you can retraumatize them. Exposure works for trauma too, but it is a different protocol with stabilization first, and it is aimed at a memory. Pushing a dysregulated nervous system into the cue repeatedly without the preparatory work teaches the body that the world is exactly as dangerous as it suspected.

Run it on an autistic adult and you are asking her to do more of the thing that is draining her, and calling the exhaustion avoidance. What actually helps there is reducing sensory and processing load, permission to leave, recovery time, and dropping the mask in the relationships where it is safe to.

Three interventions, all evidence-based, all wrong when applied to the wrong picture.

What a real assessment does about it

It takes a developmental history that goes back to early childhood, in enough detail to catch a pattern nobody labeled as trauma. It asks about sensory experience and about masking, in specific behavioral terms. It separates what the person is afraid of from what depletes them from what they have learned to expect. It uses standardized measures for each of these, and then it reconciles the measures against the history when they disagree, because they often do.

And it produces a written formulation you can read, showing why the conclusion is what it is and what was ruled out. If nobody can tell you why they landed where they landed, you have received an opinion.

It takes hours, which is the whole reason it frequently does not happen.

The Cliff Notes

You skipped down here, which for once might be the diagnostically relevant behavior. Here is the argument.

  • Social anxiety and post-traumatic stress produce almost identical avoidance from the outside, which is why short appointments confuse them.
  • Social anxiety is anticipatory and specific: fear of being judged in an event that has not yet happened. Trauma is a re-experiencing of something the body already recorded and filed as ongoing.
  • Ask what exactly the person fears will happen. Social anxiety produces a coherent answer about judgment. Trauma often produces no specific feared outcome at all, and that absence is data.
  • Social anxiety front-loads, worst before the event and easing once inside it. Trauma responses tend to fire inside the situation, triggered by a specific cue, without warning.
  • Trauma responses can be strangely situation-specific: fine in a loud crowd, unable to be in a small quiet room with one person. Social anxiety generalizes more consistently.
  • Clinicians ask about trauma and get a no, because the person is thinking of assault or combat and not of four years of an unpredictable parent.
  • Nightmares, waking at a set hour, and guarding the house at night point toward trauma. Social anxiety produces the sleeplessness of rehearsal.
  • The common real-world case is developmental trauma, autistic social exhaustion, and accurate learning from years of things going badly, tangled together.
  • To separate autistic depletion from fear, ask what leaving feels like: relief points toward anxiety, and the feeling of having moved furniture points toward depletion from masking and processing load.
  • When social situations have genuinely gone badly for years, the expectation of a bad outcome is a well-calibrated prediction. Cognitive work aimed at a distortion stalls, and the person gets called treatment-resistant.
  • Getting it wrong has a cost. Standard graded exposure can retraumatize someone with untreated PTSD, and it asks an autistic adult to do more of the thing that is draining her.
  • A real assessment takes a full developmental history, asks about sensory experience and masking in behavioral terms, uses standardized measures, and reconciles them with the history in a written formulation you can read.
  • If you have been treated for social anxiety for years and it helps some but never resolves, the question worth asking is whether anyone ever checked what the avoidance was made of.

If you have been treated for the same thing for a decade

Partial response over many years is information worth taking seriously. It usually means the treatment is working on something real, and that something else is also there.

Two things are worth doing with that. Take the questions above to whoever is treating you now, starting with what exactly you are afraid will happen, and see whether the answer changes the plan. If the picture still does not fit, ask for an evaluation that looks at anxiety, trauma, and autism together, and ask before you book whether you will get a written report that explains what was ruled out.

We do that kind of evaluation for all ages at Center for Balanced Living.

This post is educational and is not a substitute for individual clinical advice or an evaluation.
